title: IPMAT Logical Reasoning Practice Set (CAT Level)

questions.question_text: Eight friends A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H are sitting around a circular table, all facing the centre. The following is known: (i) A sits second to the right of D, and F sits between D and A. (ii) C sits immediately to the left of D. (iii) H sits immediately to the left of C. (iv) B sits opposite F. (v) E sits immediately to the left of B. Who sits opposite the person who is second to the left of D?
detailed_solution: Convention: when people face the centre, a person's LEFT is the next seat in the clockwise direction, and RIGHT is the next seat in the anticlockwise direction. Number the seats 1 to 8 clockwise.
Step 1: Place D at seat 1. 'A is second to the right of D and F sits between them' means going anticlockwise from D we meet F first, then A. So F = seat 8, A = seat 7.
Step 2: C is immediately to the left of D, so C = seat 2.
Step 3: H is immediately to the left of C, so H = seat 3.
Step 4: B sits opposite F. F is at seat 8, so the opposite seat is 4. B = seat 4.
Step 5: E is immediately to the left of B, so E = seat 5. The only person left is G, who takes seat 6.
Final clockwise order: D(1), C(2), H(3), B(4), E(5), G(6), A(7), F(8).
Step 6: Second to the left of D means two seats clockwise from D: C (first), then H (second). So the person is H at seat 3.
Step 7: The seat opposite seat 3 is seat 7, which is occupied by A.
questions.key_takeaway: Fix the direction convention first (left = clockwise when facing the centre), then anchor one person and build outward. Every clue was used exactly once and the arrangement is unique.

questions.question_text: Five friends A, B, C, D and E live on different floors of a five-storey building (floor 1 is the lowest, floor 5 is the topmost), one person per floor. Each owns a different pet: cat, dog, parrot, rabbit and fish. The following is known: (i) B lives on an odd-numbered floor, above the cat owner (B himself is not the cat owner). (ii) C lives on the topmost floor. (iii) The dog owner lives immediately between the fish owner and the parrot owner (that is, on a floor directly between theirs). (iv) A lives immediately below the fish owner. (v) E lives above B. The person living immediately above the fish owner has which pet?
detailed_solution: Step 1: From (ii), C = floor 5.
Step 2: From (i), B is on an odd floor (1, 3 or 5) and has someone (the cat owner) below him. Floor 5 is taken by C and floor 1 has no floor below it, so B = floor 3.
Step 3: From (v), E lives above B, so E is on floor 4 or 5. Floor 5 is C's, so E = floor 4.
Step 4: A and D occupy floors 1 and 2. From (iv), A lives immediately below the fish owner, so A = floor 1 and the fish owner lives on floor 2, which is D.

Step 5: From (iii), the dog owner lives directly between the fish owner (floor 2) and the parrot owner. Going up from floor 2, the dog owner is on floor 3 (B) and the parrot owner is on floor 4 (E). (Placing the dog on floor 1 would need a parrot on floor 0, which does not exist.)
Step 6: From (i), the cat owner lives below B (floor 3) and floor 2 already has the fish, so the cat owner lives on floor 1, which is A.
Step 7: The only pet left, the rabbit, belongs to C on floor 5.
Final: Floor 1 A-Cat, Floor 2 D-Fish, Floor 3 B-Dog, Floor 4 E-Parrot, Floor 5 C-Rabbit.
The person immediately above the fish owner (floor 2) lives on floor 3, which is B, who owns the Dog.
questions.key_takeaway: Start with the clues that pin down a position directly (C on floor 5), then use elimination on parity and 'above/below' conditions. Fill the floor attribute completely before assigning pets.

questions.question_text: Statements: (1) All writers are thinkers. (2) Some thinkers are artists. (3) No artist is a banker. (4) Some bankers are writers. Conclusions: I. Some thinkers are bankers. II. Some thinkers are not artists. III. Some writers are artists. IV. Some writers are not artists. Which of the conclusions logically follow from the given statements?

options.B: Only I, II and IV follow

detailed_solution: Key idea: Statement (4) is the only statement that links bankers to the other groups, so work from it.
From (4), there exist some bankers who are also writers. Call this group 'banker-writers'.
Conclusion I: Banker-writers are writers, and by (1) all writers are thinkers, so banker-writers are thinkers. They are also bankers. Hence some thinkers are bankers. I FOLLOWS.
Conclusion II: By (3), no artist is a banker, so banker-writers are not artists. They are thinkers (shown above). Hence some thinkers are not artists. II FOLLOWS.

Conclusion III: Statement (2) says some thinkers are artists, but those thinkers need not be writers. It is possible that no writer is an artist (draw the 'writers' circle inside 'thinkers' but away from the 'artists' overlap). III DOES NOT FOLLOW.
Conclusion IV: Banker-writers are writers and are not artists (by (3)). Hence some writers are not artists. IV FOLLOWS.
Therefore only I, II and IV follow.
questions.key_takeaway: In syllogism sets, combine the statement that connects the most terms with the negative statement. 'Some' conclusions need a definite overlap that is forced, not merely possible. Always test a conclusion by trying to draw a Venn diagram where it fails.

questions.question_text: On an island, every person is either a knight (always tells the truth) or a knave (always lies). Four islanders A, B, C and D make the following statements. A: 'B is a knave.' B: 'C is a knave.' C: 'A and B are both knaves.' D: 'At least two of the four of us are knaves.' Who among them are the knights?
detailed_solution: Step 1: Test the case 'A is a knight'. Then A's statement is true, so B is a knave. B's statement ('C is a knave') is then false, so C is a knight. But C says 'A and B are both knaves', which would be false since A is a knight. A knight cannot make a false statement, so this is a contradiction. Hence A is a KNAVE.
Step 2: Since A is a knave, A's statement 'B is a knave' is false, so B is a KNIGHT.
Step 3: B is a knight, so B's statement is true and C is a KNAVE.
Step 4: Check C: C says 'A and B are both knaves'. This is false because B is a knight, which is consistent with C being a knave.

Step 5: Now D. So far the knaves are A and C, so D's statement 'at least two of us are knaves' is already true. If D were a knave, the number of knaves would be 3 and the statement would still be true, but a knave cannot say something true. So D must be a KNIGHT. (If D is a knight, there are exactly 2 knaves and the statement is true, which is consistent.)
Final: Knights are B and D; knaves are A and C.
questions.key_takeaway: Pick the statement that creates the sharpest contradiction (here C's) and test one assumption fully. For statements that depend on a count that includes the speaker, check both possibilities for the speaker.

questions.question_text: In a certain code: 'A + B' means A is the mother of B; 'A - B' means A is the brother of B; 'A x B' means A is the sister of B; 'A / B' means A is the father of B. Consider the expression: P / Q x R + S - T. Based on this, P is related to T as:
detailed_solution: Decode each link of the chain in order.
P / Q: P is the father of Q.
Q x R: Q is the sister of R. So Q is female, and R is also a child of P (siblings share the same parents).
R + S: R is the mother of S. So R is female and S is a child of R. Hence S is a grandchild of P.

S - T: S is the brother of T. So S is male, and T is a sibling of S, which means T is also a child of R. Hence T is a grandchild of P (T's gender is not given, but it does not matter for this question).
Therefore P is the father of R, and R is the mother of T. P is the maternal grandfather of T.
Answer: Grandfather.
questions.key_takeaway: Convert each symbol into a relationship, note which links also reveal gender, and remember that siblings share parents. Draw a quick family tree: P at the top, Q and R in the second generation, S and T in the third generation.
